_about: Standing cargo-theft priors by corridor for sources/theft.py. Not a live feed. weekdays: 0 = Monday … 6 = Sunday; hours: [from, to) local time, may wrap midnight (context only: the engine works by day). multiplier: hand-set, modest transit effect for escorts, convoy waits and detours on the risky days (not a loss probability). figure: the published numbers the row rests on; verified = true only where the figure was read on the cited page on checked_on, false where it comes from a secondary report or could not be confirmed. Recheck each quarter against the latest Overhaul report and SESNSP 'robo a transportista' incidence.

corridors.corridor: México–Puebla–Veracruz, San Martín Texmelucan to Esperanza
corridors.figure: 68% of Puebla cargo theft is on MEX-150D; 45% of it between San Martín Texmelucan and Amozoc; 93% Monday to Friday; 51% between 18:00 and 06:00 (Q1 2024).
corridors.source: Overhaul, Understanding theft patterns in the Mexican state of Puebla

corridors.corridor: México–Querétaro (Estado de México, Hidalgo and Querétaro sections)
corridors.figure: Estado de México had 21% of cargo theft incidents in 2025, the highest of any state; the México–Querétaro road is named among the most affected routes; Friday is the peak day and 19:00–24:00 holds nearly a third of cases.
corridors.source: Overhaul, Mexico 2025 annual cargo theft report (state share); SESNSP and AMESIS figures as reported by Mexico Business News (routes, days, hours)

corridors.figure: Guanajuato is among the top three states for cargo theft (36 cases in March 2025) and rose about 2% in 2025.
corridors.source: SESNSP incidence as reported by Mexico Business News (March 2025); Overhaul, Mexico 2025 annual cargo theft report (trend)

corridors.figure: Nuevo León is named among the states affected by the 2025 rise in cargo theft; no corridor share published that we could find.
corridors.source: SESNSP and AMESIS figures as reported by Mexico Business News
